description: Calculate gross profit, net profit, profit margins and ARR to evaluate business performance and investments.
content_html:
Why Profit Calculations Matter

Revenue tells you how much a business has sold. Profit tells you how much it keeps after paying its costs. The two are very different — a business can have high revenue and still lose money if its costs are higher. Understanding profit at different levels helps managers pinpoint exactly where money is being made or lost, and whether a business is healthy enough to grow.

There are two levels of profit that every GCSE Business student must be able to calculate and interpret: gross profit and net profit. There are also two profit margin calculations — gross profit margin and net profit margin — and a method for evaluating investments called the average rate of return (ARR).

Gross Profit

Gross profit is calculated by subtracting the cost of sales from sales revenue. The cost of sales includes only the direct costs of making the goods — raw materials, bought-in components and direct labour. It does not include overheads such as rent, marketing or managers’ salaries.

Formula: Gross profit = Sales revenue − Cost of sales

Example: Hazel & Reed Homeware had sales revenue of £480,000 and a cost of sales of £190,000 in the last financial year.

Gross profit = £480,000 − £190,000 = £290,000

Key Fact

Gross profit shows how efficiently a business converts sales into profit before overheads. A high gross profit does not guarantee a healthy business if overhead costs are very large — which is why net profit is equally important.

Net Profit

Net profit is calculated by subtracting all other operating expenses (overheads and interest) from gross profit. These include rent, utilities, marketing, administrative salaries, depreciation and interest payments on loans.

Formula: Net profit = Gross profit − Other operating expenses and interest

Continuing the example: Hazel & Reed Homeware had other operating expenses of £115,000 and interest payments of £12,000.

Net profit = £290,000 − (£115,000 + £12,000) = £290,000 − £127,000 = £163,000

Raw profit figures are useful, but they don’t tell you how efficiently the business generates profit relative to its revenue. A business with £500,000 profit sounds impressive, until you discover it needed £50,000,000 in revenue to generate it. Gross profit margin and net profit margin allow comparisons between businesses and across time by expressing profit as a proportion of revenue.

Gross profit margin (%) = (Gross profit ÷ Sales revenue) × 100

Using the Hazel & Reed example: (£290,000 ÷ £480,000) × 100 = 60.42%

Net profit margin (%) = (Net profit ÷ Sales revenue) × 100

Net profit margin: (£163,000 ÷ £480,000) × 100 = 33.96%

A higher margin means the business keeps more profit per pound of revenue. Margins vary significantly by industry: supermarkets operate on very thin margins (often 1–5%), while software companies can achieve margins above 30%.

Average Rate of Return (ARR)

Average rate of return (ARR) is used to evaluate whether a capital investment is worthwhile. It tells a business what annual return (as a percentage) it can expect on the money it puts into a project — such as buying new machinery, opening a new location or developing a new product.

The formula has two steps:

Step 1: Average annual profit = (Total profit over life of investment) ÷ Number of years
where Total profit = Total returns − Initial investment cost

Step 2: ARR (%) = (Average annual profit ÷ Cost of investment) × 100

Key Fact

The most common ARR mistake is forgetting to subtract the original investment cost before calculating average annual profit. The formula uses profit (returns minus cost), not total returns. Forgetting this step overstates the ARR significantly.

ARR Worked Example

Verdant Plant Nursery is considering buying a new automated potting machine for £60,000. The machine is expected to generate total additional revenue of £96,000 over its 4-year working life, after deducting running costs.

Step 1: Total profit = £96,000 − £60,000 = £36,000
Average annual profit = £36,000 ÷ 4 = £9,000

Step 2: ARR = (£9,000 ÷ £60,000) × 100 = 15.00%

If Verdant Plant Nursery could earn 8% by keeping the money in a savings account, an ARR of 15% makes the investment look attractive. However, ARR does not account for the timing of cash flows — it treats all years as equal even if most returns come at the end of the investment’s life.

ARR is straightforward to calculate and gives a percentage that is easy to compare against a target rate of return or interest rate. However, it has real limitations. It ignores the timing of cash flows — receiving £30,000 in year one is more valuable than receiving £30,000 in year four, but ARR treats both identically. It also relies on forecasted figures, which may be inaccurate, and it does not account for the impact of inflation on future returns. Businesses therefore use ARR alongside other appraisal methods rather than in isolation.
exam_tip_html: For calculation questions, always show your working even when the question only specifies 2 marks — a method mark may be available for a correct formula. For the ARR specifically, the most frequent error in assessments is dividing by total returns instead of profit (returns minus the original investment). Write the formula first, substitute clearly, then state the final answer with its unit (£ or %). For a 6-mark “Analyse” question using ARR, don’t stop at calculating the figure — examiners want you to interpret it in context: is this ARR attractive compared to the alternative uses of the money?
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Gross profit = Revenue − Cost of sales; Net profit = Gross profit − Other operating expenses and interest. Both margins express profit as a percentage of revenue for comparison purposes.
  • ARR = (Average annual profit ÷ Cost of investment) × 100, where average annual profit = (Total profit over investment life) ÷ Number of years. Always subtract the initial investment before dividing by years.
  • ARR is useful for comparing investments but has limitations: it ignores the timing of cash flows, relies on forecasts, and should be used alongside other appraisal methods.

practice_questions.text: A business has sales revenue of £320,000 and a cost of sales of £128,000. What is the gross profit?
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks for the correct final answer of £192,000; 1 mark if the correct formula (Revenue − Cost of sales) is stated but an arithmetic error prevents the correct answer.

Formula: Gross profit = Sales revenue − Cost of sales
Substitution: £320,000 − £128,000 = £192,000

practice_questions.text: Sunvale Foods has gross profit of £75,000 and sales revenue of £250,000. Calculate the gross profit margin. Give your answer to two decimal places.
practice_questions.marks:
3 marks for the correct final answer of 30.00%.
2 marks for correct formula and correct substitution but an arithmetic error in the final step.
1 mark for the correct formula stated.

Formula: Gross profit margin (%) = (Gross profit ÷ Sales revenue) × 100
Substitution: (£75,000 ÷ £250,000) × 100 = 30.00%

practice_questions.text:
The table below shows financial data for Ridgeway Clothing Ltd.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Sales revenue | £500,000 |
| Cost of sales | £200,000 |
| Other operating expenses | £140,000 |
| Interest payments | £10,000 |

Identify the net profit margin for Ridgeway Clothing Ltd.

Harbour Lane Gym is considering investing £40,000 in new fitness equipment. The equipment is expected to generate total additional profit of £56,000 over four years. Calculate the average rate of return (ARR) for this investment. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
3 marks for the correct final answer of 40.00%.
2 marks for correctly calculating average annual profit (£4,000) but making an error in the final ARR step.
1 mark for correctly identifying that total profit = £56,000 − £40,000 = £16,000.

Step 1: Total profit = £56,000 − £40,000 = £16,000
Average annual profit = £16,000 ÷ 4 = £4,000
Step 2: ARR = (£4,000 ÷ £40,000) × 100 = 10.00%

Note: The question states 'total additional profit of £56,000' — no deduction of the initial investment is needed before dividing by years because the figure is already profit. ARR = (£56,000 ÷ 4 ÷ £40,000) × 100 = (£14,000 ÷ £40,000) × 100 = 35.00%.

Accept either interpretation if clearly shown: full marks for 35.00% with correct working (interpreting £56,000 as total returns) or for 10.00% with correct working (interpreting £56,000 as total profit after deducting investment). Mark the method, not just the answer.

practice_questions.text:
Cobble Lane Coffee has two cafés in Manchester. The owner is comparing two investment options:

Option A: Refurbish the larger café at a cost of £50,000. Expected total returns over 5 years: £85,000.
Option B: Open a pop-up stall at a cost of £20,000. Expected total returns over 4 years: £36,000.

Analyse which investment option offers the better average rate of return for Cobble Lane Coffee.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks per investment option (1 for correct ARR calculation + 1 for interpretation + 1 for contextual development).

Option A ARR: Total profit = £85,000 − £50,000 = £35,000. Average annual profit = £35,000 ÷ 5 = £7,000. ARR = (£7,000 ÷ £50,000) × 100 = 14.00%.

Option B ARR: Total profit = £36,000 − £20,000 = £16,000. Average annual profit = £16,000 ÷ 4 = £4,000. ARR = (£4,000 ÷ £20,000) × 100 = 20.00%.

Option B has a higher ARR (20% vs 14%). Contextual development: the pop-up stall generates a better return per pound invested. However, Option A generates more total profit (£35,000 vs £16,000) and may better suit Cobble Lane Coffee's growth ambitions in Manchester. The analysis should acknowledge that ARR does not capture total profit scale or cash flow timing.

6 marks for correct calculations for both options plus developed contextual analysis comparing both. 4 marks for both correct calculations with limited context. 2 marks for one correct calculation.

practice_questions.text:
Fenwick Street Bakery had the following financial results last year:

- Sales revenue: £180,000
- Cost of sales: £72,000
- Other operating expenses: £54,000
- Interest payments: £6,000

The owner is considering investing £30,000 in new baking equipment. The equipment is expected to generate total additional profit of £24,000 over 4 years. Justify a recommendation on whether Fenwick Street Bakery should make this investment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): Recommendation is clearly stated and grounded in Fenwick Street Bakery's specific financial position. Candidate calculates the ARR correctly (ARR: total profit = £24,000; average annual profit = £6,000; ARR = £6,000 ÷ £30,000 × 100 = 20.00%). Also calculates the net profit margin: gross profit = £180,000 − £72,000 = £108,000; net profit = £108,000 − £54,000 − £6,000 = £48,000; net profit margin = 48,000 ÷ 180,000 × 100 = 26.67%. Uses both figures analytically: 20% ARR is attractive if the bakery can spare £30,000 (26.67% net margin suggests reasonable profitability). Addresses the strongest counter-argument (e.g. the investment ties up cash for 4 years; the bakery's net profit of £48,000 means £30,000 is a significant proportion of annual profit). Conclusion adds evaluative judgement.

Secure (7–9 marks): Calculates ARR correctly and links it to a recommendation with some reference to the bakery's financial data. Counter-argument present but less developed.

Developing (4–6 marks): May calculate ARR but analysis is general. Recommendation may not be clearly justified using both financial measures.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Limited calculations; recommendation present but unsupported.

knowledge_checks.q: Which formula correctly calculates gross profit?
options: Sales revenue minus all operating expenses
Sales revenue minus cost of sales
Cost of sales minus sales revenue

knowledge_checks.q: A business has an ARR of 12%. What does this tell the owner?
options: The business makes 12p profit for every £1 of sales revenue
The investment returns an average of 12% of the investment cost per year as profit
The business's gross profit margin is 12%
The business needs 12 years to recover the investment

knowledge_checks.q: Net profit = Gross profit minus other operating expenses and _____.
The average rate of return expresses the average annual _____ as a percentage of the initial investment cost.
Match each formula to the correct financial measure:

flashcard_questions.a: Gross profit − other operating expenses and interest.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a higher net profit margin indicate?
flashcard_questions.a: The business keeps more profit from each pound of revenue after all costs.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the average rate of return (ARR)?
flashcard_questions.a: An investment appraisal method expressing average annual profit as a percentage of the investment cost.

flashcard_questions.q: How is average annual profit calculated for ARR?
flashcard_questions.a: Total profit over the investment's life divided by the number of years.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the most common ARR calculation error?
flashcard_questions.a: Forgetting to subtract the initial investment before calculating average annual profit.
The direct costs of making goods sold, such as raw materials and direct labour.

flashcard_questions.q: Why can a business with high gross profit still have low net profit?
flashcard_questions.a: If its overhead costs (rent, wages, marketing) are very high, they consume most of the gross profit.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one limitation of ARR as an investment appraisal method.
flashcard_questions.a: It ignores the timing of cash flows, treating all years of returns as equal.

glossary_terms.definition: Revenue minus the cost of sales (the direct costs of producing the goods or services sold).
Gross profit minus all other operating expenses and interest, representing the profit remaining after all costs have been deducted.
Gross profit expressed as a percentage of sales revenue.
Net profit expressed as a percentage of sales revenue.
An investment appraisal method that expresses the average annual profit from an investment as a percentage of the initial investment cost.
The direct costs of producing the goods or services sold, including raw materials and direct labour, but excluding overheads.
